title: Wanting to Save the World Is No Excuse for a Monopoly Agreement
dek: AI labs want to jointly slow down model development, but four giants sitting down to talk about deceleration is, legally, a textbook antitrust conspiracy — wanting to save the world is not a defense.
why: Three segments: the insider-trading evidentiary problem, Dario's deceleration memo, and pension privatization. Medium information density; the last two segments are worth more.
who: Founders and investors interested in the business logic of the AI race, insider-trading evidence-gathering, and the evolution of the US retirement system.
skip: The opening chit-chat about Absalom, Absalom and reading habits can be skipped.

points.h: Suing a hundred John Does doesn't fly with the judge
points.body: Susquehanna spotted heavy buying of short-dated put options in Chinese brokerage stocks before cross-border trading was restricted, so it sued 100 John Does to freeze the accounts. But the judge denied the preliminary injunction: it could not be proven that all 100 were conspiring to trade on inside information. Levine's breakdown is that only a tiny few may have actually gotten the inside tip, while the rest just saw the tape move and piled in — and piling into publicly visible price moves is itself entirely legal. The party that can actually figure out who is who is the securities regulator, not the market maker that got picked off.

points.h: The market maker's losses may not be that big
points.body: Susquehanna claims it lost about $70 million on those puts, but Levine points out that is only half the story: as an options market maker, after selling puts it would normally hedge immediately, possibly by shorting the stock, or by buying puts back from another client or another market maker. If Citadel Securities and Susquehanna were both selling and both buying that day, they were effectively betting against each other and should in theory be suing each other. So the "lost $70 million" figure obscures the fact that they were also hedging, and may even have been net up on the day.

points.h: Not training new models is actually more profitable
points.body: Levine offers a counterintuitive business logic: model capability now runs ahead of deployment in many domains, and Anthropic and OpenAI are working with private equity firms to push AI into enterprises. If they stopped model development for a year, they could make a lot of money selling existing models, with quite good unit economics. But competitive pressure forces every frontier lab to keep burning huge sums training the next model — both to win customers on the leaderboard and to win researchers, because researchers want to go to the best lab. So "slowing down" is good for business, but no one dares unilaterally lay down the weapon.

points.h: Four of them sitting down to talk deceleration is collusion
points.body: Since no one dares slow down unilaterally, could the four frontier labs sit down and reach an agreement? Levine says that is legally a classic antitrust conspiracy — like the case in which BlackRock was sued by several state attorneys general: ESG investors got coal companies to produce less coal on the grounds that global warming is bad for humanity, but the effect was higher coal prices, making them the OPEC of coal. The line in the ruling is "wanting to save the world is no excuse for an antitrust conspiracy." Dario's memo also adds a footnote saying antitrust law would need to be appropriately amended before they would be allowed to sit in a room and discuss shutting down the killer robots.

points.h: The founding documents are all handwritten by humans
points.body: Sylvia read Kevin Roos's book on the AGI race (out October 6; she had a pre-read copy) and found a contrast: every dramatic turning point in the book corresponds to a human handwritten memo — Dario's Pacing the Frontier, the Say AGI memo, and so on. Yet what everyone discusses now is "was this written by AI." Reading Dario's memo, she instinctively wondered "did Claude write this," and concluded it did not read like AI at all — these people are philosophers writing original founding texts. But the next generation will probably just ask Claude what to do.

points.h: A 401k has no funding gap, only a balance that's too small
points.body: A pension is a future cash flow the company has promised, and the company must invest to match that liability; invest wrong and there is a funding gap, which is why ERISA steps in to govern pension insolvency. A 401k is not a promised cash flow, just a pool of money: if stocks fall, they fall, and there is no such thing on the books as a "billion-dollar funding gap," only "the number in your account is lower than you want." This eliminates concentration risk — with a 401k, pension insolvency can never happen. The cost is that risk shifts from the company to the individual.

points.h: Pensions were actually great clients for Wall Street
points.body: The popular story is that the shift from pensions to 401ks was good for Wall Street, because it turned people who would retire on a pension into retail clients trading their own accounts. Levine pushes back: a pension is itself an excellent client for Wall Street, because its time horizon is long and it can make the spicy investments retail investors won't touch — private equity, private credit. The 401k, over these decades, became cheap index funds, and retail investors actually pay extremely low fees. So now the financial industry is pushing to "revive the pension," stuffing private assets into retirement accounts, because charging one basis point on a public equity index earns you nothing.

points.h: Retail says long-term but their hands want liquidity
points.body: Private credit BDCs raise money from retail investors on the logic that "you have a 30-year horizon, you don't need liquidity, you should take the liquidity premium." Then this year software companies delivered bad news, investors rushed to redeem, and the BDCs could only say they would allow just 5% of people to redeem each quarter. Levine calls it "psychological liquidity mismatch": the fund really is making long-term investments and really should not sell long-term assets to meet redemptions; but retail investors psychologically want more liquidity than the fund offers. In theory, selling private assets to retirement savers is right; in practice, it is very hard.
